message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties** | Property | Value / Description | |----------|---------------------| | **Atomic Number** | 1 | | **Symbol** | H | | **Isotopic Forms** |
  • ¹H (protium) – most abundant (~99.98 %)
  • ²H (deuterium) – ~0.02 % natural abundance; heavier isotope used in nuclear fusion research.
  • ³H (tritium) – radioactive, half‑life ≈12.32 yr; produced artificially or via neutron capture.
| | **Electron Configuration** | 1s¹ | | **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 (highest among elements) | | **First Ionisation Energy** | 1312 kJ/mol (high due to single valence electron) | | **Second Ionisation Energy** | 2857 kJ/mol (very high because it would remove the second proton from He core) | | **Molecular Form at STP** | Diatomic gas \( \mathrm{H_2}\). Each molecule has two covalent bonds with bond dissociation energy ≈436 kJ/mol. | | **Boiling Point** | −252.9 °C (−423.8 °F); very low due to weak London dispersion forces between molecules. | | **Melting Point** | −259.16 °C (≈14 K above absolute zero). | | **Density** | 0.08988 g/L at 25 °C (lowest of all gases). | | **Specific Heat Capacity (gas)** | 28.836 J/(mol·K) at constant pressure. | | **Solubility in Water** | Very limited (<0.0015 mol/kg at room temperature). Dissolves more readily under acidic conditions forming hydronium ions. | | **Reactivity** | Extremely reactive; forms acids when dissolved in water (\( \mathrm{H^+ + OH^- → H_2O}\)). Combines with oxygen to form water explosively. Reacts with halogens, metals, nonmetals, and many organic compounds. | | **Bonding Behavior** | Typically forms one covalent bond per atom. In dihydrogen, each H shares its lone electron pair. Can act as both donor (in acid–base reactions) and acceptor (forming hydrates). | | **Oxidation States** | Commonly +1 (as in salts like NaCl, CaF₂) and -1 (rare, e.g., Li⁻ in lithium metal fluoride). In molecular species, neutral state (0). | | **Acidity/Base Strength** | As a cationic species (e.g., \( \mathrm{H^+}\)), extremely strong acid. As a radical or negative ion, behaves as a base only in specialized contexts. | | **Spectroscopic Features** | Strong absorption lines in UV-visible region (Balmer series). Infrared active vibrational mode around 4400 cm⁻¹ for H₂. | | **Astrophysical Significance** | Most abundant element in universe; fuels stellar nucleosynthesis via proton-proton chain and CNO cycle. Emits characteristic spectral lines observed in stars and interstellar clouds. | | **Industrial Uses** | Fuel cell technology, ammonia synthesis (Haber process), petroleum refining, semiconductor manufacturing, rocket propellant (LH₂/LOX). | | **Safety Notes** | Highly flammable; explosive mixtures with air/O₂. Requires careful handling—use inert atmosphere or controlled environments. | --- ### Quick Takeaways * **Lightest Element:** Atomic mass ≈1 u; lowest density of any elemental gas. * **Strong Electronegativity:** Highest among elements, making it highly effective at attracting electrons. * **High Ionisation Energies:** Removing even the first electron requires substantial energy. * **Low Boiling/Melting Points:** Makes liquid hydrogen cryogenic; essential for certain industrial processes. * **Versatile Chemistry:** Acts as both oxidant and reductant depending on context; central player in acid-base chemistry and combustion. Feel free to dive deeper into any specific aspect!
